items.text:
'Humanitarian mission' for Kostiantynivka: Is it a trap?
November 19, 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he says, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.
Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.
In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine says the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult."
Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and said that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.
What is the situation for civilians?
Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, said Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.
Local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.
"Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.
Humanitarian proposals as leverage
Kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he said, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.
Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and said the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.
Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," said Popovych.
Ceasefire as military tactic
After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff announced that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.
Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.
"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.
How should Kyiv respond to Moscow's proposal?
Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers currently at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.
Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.
The human rights activist said that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.

Tottenham winger
items.text:
Shevchenko accuses Mudryk camp of 'baseless slander'
- Published
Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for an employee of the country's football federation to "falsely" take the blame for the winger's positive drugs test.
Tottenham winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.
The 25-year-old said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.
In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk firmly placed the blame for his 20-month absence from the sport on his national association, which has led to Shevchenko's response.
In a statement, former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko, who is now president of the UAF, said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally" and called on the player to retract his words.
He added: "His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample.
"The UAF refused, as such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work."
He added that "numerous investigations and audits" undertaken as part of the case were unable to shed light on when or where the substance entered Mudryk's system.
In his interview Mudryk also claimed Shevchenko had offered him little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and said its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.
However, Shevchenko went on to say that national team staff had complied with a request from Chelsea not to provide Mudryk with any medication while on international duty.
And he also challenged the former Shakhtar Donetsk forward to provide evidence "to back up his words".
"Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps," Shevchenko added.
"These were the exact people who monitored his regimen and recovery, and helped him with his daily routine.
"The UAF completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk's representatives with the information they requested and remained in contact with those working on the case.
"I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism.
"If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question."
BBC Sport has contacted Mudryk's representatives for comment.

A three-way meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States has yielded a number of commitments.

FIA announce introduction of full-time F1 stewards from 2027 ahead of Las Vegas Grand Prix
Formula 1's governing body, the FIA, has revealed full-time stewards will be used for the first time from next year; watch the Las Vegas GP weekend on Sky Sports F1, with Friday's practice sessions at 12.30am and 4pm
Thursday 19 November 2026 20:45, UK
The FIA has announced it will introduce full-time Formula 1 stewards from 2027 with the aim of having "greater consistency in decision-making".
The use of full-time stewards has been a consistent talking point in F1 as different stewards, who adjudicate all racing and technical matters on a race weekend, are used at each event over the season.
There has been an argument that this can lead to inconsistencies in decision-making when it comes to imposing penalties, or the severity of a penalty.

But the FIA announced on Thursday, ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, they will begin to recruit full-time stewards with a phased introduction from next year with the aim of establishing 12-15 full-time stewards over the coming years.
Currently, there are four stewards drawn from a large FIA pool of officials and one of those is a former racing driver. The new structure will continue to use the knowledge of driver stewards at each event and the FIA say full-time stewards will "allow for deeper implementation of best practice and greater consistency in decision-making".
The news comes a month after the opening of the FIA Remote Operations Centre at Biggin Hill in the UK, following a reorganisation of Race Control in 2022 after the controversial 2021 season which saw Max Verstappen overtake Lewis Hamilton on the last lap of the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.
"This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport," said FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.
"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula One World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport.
"Following the milestone opening of the new FIA Remote Operations Centre and strengthening of officiating development through initiatives such as the FIA High Performance Programme, this development will help to build greater expertise and continuity within our stewarding structure, strengthening our ability to review and improve regulations, support the development of future officials and ensure the highest standards of consistent officiating across all our championships."

items.title: Trump’s case against NYT and Penguin Random House may proceed: Judge
items.summary:
Trump’s case against NYT and Penguin Random House may proceed: Judge
The lawsuit cited a book about Trump by two NYT reporters and what it said were ‘false, malicious, defamatory’ articles.
A federal judge has said United States President Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The New York Times
items.text:
Trump’s case against NYT and Penguin Random House may proceed: Judge
The lawsuit cited a book about Trump by two NYT reporters and what it said were ‘false, malicious, defamatory’ articles.
A federal judge has said United States President Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The New York Times and book publisher Penguin Random House may proceed, a victory for Trump in his legal campaign against media companies he accuses of treating him unfairly.
US District Judge Steven Merryday, an appointee of former President George HW Bush, handed down the ruling in federal court in Tampa, Florida, on Thursday.
Trump has filed several lawsuits against media companies since 2024, alleging they defamed him or fraudulently misled the public with false coverage. His critics have denounced the lawsuits as attacks on the free press.
The lawsuit against The New York Times and Penguin Random House cited a book about Trump by two New York Times reporters and what it characterised as “false, malicious, defamatory, and disparaging” articles that he says were aimed at sabotaging his chances in the 2024 presidential election, which he won.
The Times and Penguin have denied defaming Trump and said in a court filing that his case is legally flawed and aimed at scoring political points.
Representatives for The New York Times, Penguin Random House and Trump’s personal lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Merryday threw out two of Trump’s claims but said the rest of his complaint plausibly alleged that statements accusing Trump of “planning and perpetrating complex crimes” were “based on incomplete, minimal information”.
The lawsuit against The Times and Penguin concerned two articles and a book that cast doubts on his origin story as a savvy businessman who ascended in the real estate and entertainment industries.
Trump cited 22 statements from the book by Times journalist Peter Baker titled For Trump, a Lifetime of Scandals Heads Toward a Moment of Judgment, and 12 from the articles by Susanne Craig and Russ Buettner.
They include assertions about Trump’s role in creating his hit reality TV show The Apprentice, his inheritance from his father, his business ventures and upbringing in New York City.
The Times and Penguin said in a motion to dismiss that Trump’s lawsuit failed to explain how the statements were defamatory and included subjective opinions that cannot be proven true or false.
‘Press freedom crisis’
The latest victory comes days after another judge allowed Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC to move forward. That civil case alleges that the British broadcaster deceptively edited a documentary on the January 6, 2021, riots on Capitol Hill to damage Trump’s reputation.
Trump, since resuming office last year, has undertaken a wider pressure campaign against the media and coverage he disagrees with. He has an ongoing $10bn lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal that he refiled in May after it had been dismissed. In September, he moved to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House and its press pool – a blanket ban a federal judge later blocked.
The US has fallen to a “historic low” in the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) annual press freedom tracker, continuing a decade-long decline, the organisation said earlier this year in its annual report.
While the US, during the first year of Trump’s second term, remained in the “problematic” category, it dropped seven places from 57th in the world to 64th.
In a statement, Clayton Weimers, executive director of RSF’s North America office, said at the time that the US was experiencing a “press freedom crisis”.
“Trump and his administration have carried out a coordinated war on press freedom since the day he took office, and we will live with the consequences for years to come,” he said.

items.text:
Macron urges Ukraine's allies to 'reopen the question' of NATO membership
French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday called for Ukraine's allies to speed up the delivery of urgently needed air defence systems and urged them to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's NATO membership after talks in Berlin aimed at reaffirming European support for Kyiv.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Ukraine's allies met Thursday for a "Coalition of the Willing" summit in Berlin with President Volodymyr Zelensky to stress solid wartime support for Kyiv and to push for a European role in any future peace talks.
Co-hosting the talks with the leaders of Germany and the UK, French President Emmanuel Macron called on Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the air defence systems it needs, and urged them to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's NATO membership.
Read moreUkraine's allies meet in Berlin to rally support for Kyiv after Trump-Putin-Xi talks
"Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine's accession to NATO," Macron said in Berlin.
"Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now," he insisted, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.
The Berlin summit, with more than 25 leaders, took place only hours after the unprecedented three-way summit between US President Donald Trump, Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China.
Read moreWhat to know about Xi, Putin and Trump's historic trilateral summit
Macron said a peace declaration agreed by Trump, Putin and Xi in China "does not lead to a reorganisation of the world".
"Today, if there is one critical factor in Europe's reorganisation, its security, it is precisely the meeting that took place in Berlin," he said.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham added: "I hope that message is heard very clearly in Moscow. For as long as it takes, we will be there at the side of Ukraine and we will not falter."
Co-hosting the talks, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he expected new Ukraine peace talks to "take place soon", with Europe now set to have a seat at the table alongside the United States, Russia and Ukraine.
Merz did not give a date and added that "we are looking for locations on neutral ground", naming the United Arab Emirates as a possible location.
Trump called into the Berlin talks from aboard Air Force One on his way back from Shenzhen, said US envoy Jared Kushner, who attended the Berlin gathering with fellow special envoy Steve Witkoff.
Kushner said Trump supported Europe's involvement in a peace deal on Ukraine and that the US-European position was growing "much closer".
Trump's son-in-law added that the US president was open to extending to Ukraine a security guarantee similar to NATO's mutual defence clause, but stressed that Washington has to protect its interests.
"From America's perspective, giving an Article Five-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal," he said. "And I think that that's something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America's interest to do that."
Asked about the NATO question later, Ukraine's Zelensky said that a real security guarantee for Ukraine would be having US or European "forces, bases" on its territory.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.text:
Senate Republicans in US reject measure to limit Trump’s war powers in Iran
The resolution was defeated 51-48. Three Republicans broke rank, voting against the measure.
United States Senate Republicans have voted against a measure that would have required President Donald Trump to end the war in Iran or seek congressional approval to continue military action, reaffirming their support for the conflict despite recent electoral losses widely attributed in part to public opposition to the war.
The resolution was defeated on Thursday 51 to 48. Senators voted largely along party lines. In June, the House of Representatives passed it 215 to 208.
Three Republicans – Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky – voted with Democrats in favour of the measure. Only one Democrat, Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, voted against it.
Democratic Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia, a longtime advocate for restoring Congress’s constitutional authority over decisions to go to war, urged lawmakers to support the resolution. He argued that the election results reflected widespread dissatisfaction with the conflict and the rising cost of food, fuel and other goods.
“The unpopularity was made absolutely, manifestly clear in the election results of November 3,” Kaine said ahead of the vote.

items.text:
Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the gadget earlier this year and said the company expected to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but he didn’t provide a price at the time.
Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300
The Information has reported a potential price for the Muse Charm, which is expected to ship in time for the holidays.
When he announced the Muse Charm, Zuckerberg said that the company had “packed the whole Muse experience,” including real-time voice and avatar technology, into the gadget. It has a fingerprint sensor, and you can tap it to be able to talk to a Muse AI agent without unlocking a phone or opening an app. The Information reports that the Muse Charm will come with a free 12-month 5G data plan from Verizon.
Spokesperson Tyler Yee wrote to The Information that “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” When reached for comment by The Verge, Yee provided the same statement.
The company is also working on a smartwatch, The Information says, but a launch for that has been pushed to 2027 as Meta tries to get Muse Charm out the door.
Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm.
Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.

items.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
items.summary: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huan
items.text:
Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security.
U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported.
The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.
By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee.
The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.
As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.
November 17, 2026: Nvidia posts strong quarterly earnings, says it does not plan to reinstate Huang
Nvidia reported its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, which beat Wall Street expectations with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year. Despite the unknowns the company faces without Huang involved, interim CEO Colette Kress said that full-year revenue is also on track to exceed expectations. The company also plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year, indicating confidence that this unexpected leadership change won’t get in the way of its trajectory.
“We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress said. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.”
Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones affirmed that the company is not considering reinstating Huang. Kress also said that Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.
November 17, 2026: Huang says he sees ‘outpouring’ of calls for him to return, says he ‘would be honored’ to return as CEO
Jensen Huang posted his first public statement since he admitted to having an extramarital affair more than a week earlier.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.
Many of Huang’s colleagues in the tech industry, including Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey, and Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan, have called for his return.
November 13, 2026: Huang was not confident in his successor, Colette Kress; reports describe Huang as ‘broken’
More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia.
Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.”

items.text:
Frank happy to be 'back in the circus' at Palace
- Published
Thomas Frank is happy to be "back in the circus" after speaking at his first news conference as Crystal Palace manager.
The 53-year-old, who was appointed on a two-and-a-half-year deal on Monday, has been out of worked since he was sacked by Tottenham in February, less than eight months after taking the job.
But, rather than dwell on that disappointment, Frank hopes to use it as a learning exeprience as he attempts to improve Palace's fortunes and lift them off the bottom of the Premier League table.
"If you don't learn from any of your jobs, I don't think you reflect, I don't think you improve, and I don't think you get better," said Frank.
"Of course there's a lot of things I have been reflecting over. The details, that will be for another time, but I can say I've learned, definitely."
The Dane said he could easily have extended his break from football, which he used to travel to Japan and Australia, as well as "visiting friends and family, eating too well [and] drinking too much wine" back in his homeland.
"I was very aware I didn't want to do anything in the summer. I put a statement out there, I needed more time," he added.
"I can actually, honestly say I would have been fine if it was three, four, five, six, seven months more, because it's good to be back in the circus, but it's also unbelievably good not to be in, especially if you enjoy life, which I do.
"I was spending time with family and friends and doing all that, but I think the club, the way Palace is, how well Steve Parish especially spoke about the club and ideas, Matt Hobbs and Iain Moody and these guys, too, helped convince me it was a good idea.
"I'm a little bit surprised by this feeling I have in the body, how good it feels."
- How Frank can restore reputation and save Crystal Palace 
  - Published3 days ago
Frank's Palace reign begins with a trip to Coventry City on Saturday (15:00 GMT) and he says he returns to the dugout unbruised despite the way his stint at Spurs ended.
"I think we all have an ego," the former Brentford boss said. "Some are better at controlling it than others. For me, it's not the critics, it's more what I can learn, what I can prove, how I can get better.
"There's a lot of clever people out there, but the interesting thing is they only know 10 per cent of the truth. That's a tenth of the truth at Brentford, there's a tenth of the truth at Tottenham, and that's just the way it is.
"If you can't handle that as a coach or a player, then you shouldn't be in this business, and I'm very happy to be back in the game."

items.text:
Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
- Published
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.
After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.
Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.
The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.
He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.
Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.
While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.
Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.
In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.
The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.
It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.
'Recognition of our suffering'
The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."
Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".
Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".
To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.
Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.
Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.
Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.
However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.
The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.
Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.

items.text:
Google is updating its homepage to include AI searches. In a post on X, Google’s vice president of product, Robby Stein, shows how you can now open a sidebar to view and continue your AI chats.
Google is putting AI chats right on the homepage
You can now view your recent AI searches by opening the sidebar on Google’s homepage.
Based on the GIF shared by Stein, it looks like you can open the sidebar by clicking the gray bar that appears on the left side of your screen. From there, Google will show a list of the searches you’ve made using AI Mode, along with the ability to start a new thread, search your threads, or connect a Gemini Notebook.
It’s a big change for Google’s homepage, which has long presented you with a single bar to kick off your web search. Stein says Google is making the change because “people are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done,” adding that “in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.”

The US defence secretary praised security cooperation with Colombia as the country joins the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition.

items.text:
‘On the same page’: Hegseth hails US ties with Colombia’s de la Espriella
The US defence secretary praised security cooperation with Colombia as the country joins the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition.
Bogota, Colombia – United States Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has hailed the White House’s close alliance with far-right Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella during a brief visit to the capital, Bogota.
The US envoy met with top officials on Wednesday to discuss cooperation against organised crime and drug trafficking in the region.
They also announced Colombia as the likely host of next year’s meeting of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (AC3).
“It was an excellent meeting, and we’re completely on the same page. And I think the reason we’re on the same page is because both of our countries are led by strong, clear leaders,” Hegseth told reporters on Wednesday.
The US defence secretary landed at an Air Force base in Bogota around 1pm local time (18:00 GMT) Wednesday, before having a closed-door meeting with Colombian Defence Minister Jorge Mora and the General Commander of the Armed Forces Erik Rodriguez.
The military leaders discussed the difficulties of combatting the armed groups active in Colombia, particularly along the border with Venezuela, and the mounting challenge posed by their use of advanced drones, according to local media reports.
De la Espriella, a political outsider, was elected on a promise to crush Colombia’s cartels through military force. Sergio Guzman, director of Colombia Risk Analysis, a political risk consultancy, said the president will require US support to achieve his goals.
“Colombia’s fiscal situation suggests that the government needs as much assistance as it can get,” argued the analyst.
Though no new funding commitments materialised during the visit, Hegseth presided over the formal delivery of a Lockheed C-130 Hercules plane, used to transport troops and cargo, to the Colombian Air Force.
“We’ve partnered more deeply with Colombia than ever before, and now we are just enhancing that cooperation and that partnership,” Hegseth told reporters.
Standing next to Hegseth at a news conference, Mora also announced that Colombia would host next year’s meeting of the AC3, also known as the Shield of the Americas.
Launched in March, the AC3 serves as an alliance of US-aligned nations in Latin America and the Caribbean, aimed at combatting organised crime through a military-centred approach.
Colombia only recently joined the coalition when de la Espriella – who was endorsed by Trump – took power in August, replacing leftist Gustavo Petro, who regularly clashed with the White House.
The Trump administration has been pressuring members of the alliance to allow US strikes on their territory, as it seeks to expand its bombing campaign against suspected drug vessels in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific to land operations.
Though Hegseth announced at an August AC3 summit in Panama that de la Espriella had authorised joint military operations, The New York Times reported yesterday that the Colombian president had since shot down the idea of direct US intervention in Colombia.
The New York Times also reported that Hegseth shortened his visit to Colombia as a result of the rejection of a bilateral military agreement.
Both Hegseth and de la Espriella described the report as “false”, highlighting ongoing close collaboration between the two militaries.
But de la Espriella noted that the move would require congressional approval, something that would be difficult, given unfavourable public opinion.
Guzman noted that Colombia’s rejection of direct US strikes likely deals a blow to the White House’s hopes for direct intervention against drug traffickers.
“Colombia is at the centre, the keystone of the strategy. So that’s quite a disappointment for [the Trump administration], I can imagine,” he said.
Hegseth also visited Venezuela on Wednesday, where he signed a bilateral deal pledging US military support for Caracas. He later departed Colombia for Ecuador and is also scheduled to make a brief stop in Honduras.

items.title: Thomas Frank admits he has a point to prove after taking reins at Crystal Palace
items.summary:
Thomas Frank has admitted he has a point to prove on his return to management as he aims to steer Crystal Palace away from relegation trouble after taking over as manager.
The Dane was confirmed as Pierre Sage’s successor on Monday with Palace at the bottom of the table after 10 matches having conce
items.text:
Thomas Frank has admitted he has a point to prove on his return to management as he aims to steer Crystal Palace away from relegation trouble after taking over as manager.
The Dane was confirmed as Pierre Sage’s successor on Monday with Palace at the bottom of the table after 10 matches having conceded 24 goals – the most in the Premier League. They face a crucial trip to Coventry on Saturday and Frank admitted he had been “surprised about how good it feels” after returning to work for the first time since being sacked by Tottenham in February.
The 53-year-old spent most of the intervening period travelling, working as a pundit at the World Cup and taking in trips to Japan, Australia and his native Denmark, where he was visiting friends and family when he received the SOS call from Palace last week. Frank previously spent seven years in charge of Brentford but left Spurs after just eight months with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history. He believes he has learned from that experience.
“I think you’ve all got an ego,” he said. “Some are better at controlling it than others. For me, it’s not the critics. It’s more what I can bring myself, what I can learn, what I can prove, how I can get better. I think that’s the big thing.
“In this world there’s a lot of clever people out there. But they only know a 10th of the truth. And that’s a 10th of the truth at Brentford and a 10th of the truth at Tottenham. That’s just the way it is – if you can’t handle that as a coach or a player or whatever, then you shouldn’t be in this business. I’m just very happy to be back in the game, very happy to be in a fantastic club, at Palace, where you walk in the door and you just feel the energy. You feel the people. It just feels good.”
Frank said he is planning to pick Roy Hodgson’s brains in the coming days after recalling a conversation they had when the former England and Palace manager was still at Selhurst Park.
“I was thinking, does it ever go away? The worry, do you get more relaxed about everything?” he asked Hodgson. “‘No chance, it’s impossible.’ I thought it would have been a little bit easier with age and experience. But in a way can’t help ourselves. I know what I want and the direction we should go in.”
Justin Cochrane – one of Thomas Tuchel’s assistants for England – has joined as first-team coach and took his first session with Palace on Monday less than 24 hours after the Nations League victory over Spain in Madrid. He is expected to be joined on Palace’s backroom staff by Bernardo Cueva, with Frank confirming that a deal with Chelsea is “very close” for the Mexican. Both worked with Frank at Brentford, where he spent almost nine years as an assistant and then manager. He is also hoping to add Andreas Georgson from Tottenham, who has been credited for his prowess on set-pieces: an area that Palace have struggled with for some time.

items.title: Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days
items.summary:
Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days
A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C. arch for two weeks, another short-term victory for those who don't want to see the 250-foot structure break ground.
D.C. District Judge
items.text:
Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days
A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C. arch for two weeks, another short-term victory for those who don't want to see the 250-foot structure break ground.
D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her temporary restraining order on Wednesday, the day before it was set to expire. She originally stepped in to block construction on the night of Nov. 5, after the National Capital Planning Commission and National Park Service gave the arch final approval and the Trump administration said construction could begin imminently.
Chutkan's new five-page order prevents the administration from "initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at Memorial Circle through Dec. 3.
"The judge's order recognizes that the conditions that called for emergency relief two weeks ago remain unchanged," Nick Sansone, the Public Citizen attorney representing the original plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in a statement.
The extension gives Chutkan more time to consider plaintiffs' request for a longer-term preliminary injunction, which would prohibit construction as the lawsuit against the arch plays out.
That lawsuit started earlier this year with a challenge from a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, but has expanded in recent weeks.
In late October, the governments of D.C. and Virginia filed another lawsuit, which was combined with the original. And nine members of the Kennedy family joined the fight last week, saying the arch will block historic sightlines and cast shadows over the graves of John F. Kennedy and others at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.
"This is one man who wants to build this arch. He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved," Max Kennedy, a son of Robert F. Kennedy, told NPR's All Things Considered.
Opposition to the arch — from area residents, veterans, local officials, Democratic lawmakers and more — has grown in recent months as the structure hurtled through the federal approval process.
Critics take issue with the arch's scale and location, saying it would interrupt the solemn and historic vista between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Plaintiffs argue the structure violates several laws — including the Commemorative Works Act and D.C.'s Height of Buildings Act — and is fundamentally illegal without approval from Congress.
The Trump administration has not sought that approval, arguing the arch is covered by Congress' authorization in 1925 of a pair of 166-foot columns at the same location, which were never built.
In court filings and a recently unveiled website, the administration characterizes building the arch as a matter of urgency — both to complete that century-old vision and to facilitate national security. Trump said in September that the arch would double as a military complex, but the plans that got final approval this month don't include any details to that effect.
In a declaration this week, Ricky Buria, chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, told the court that the agency is "currently in the planning process to determine how to integrate national defense uses … into the Arch without changing the existing plans for the Arch."
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR on Thursday that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."
The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has pursued with vigor in his second term. Some of them, like the White House ballroom and Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, are well underway. Others, like the Kennedy Center closure and East Potomac golf course redevelopment, are held up by various legal challenges.
Democrats have said they will use their forthcoming majority in Congress to push back on Trump's construction agenda, including by blocking federal funding. But experts say the fate of many of these projects will ultimately be up to the court.
'Time is of the essence' at East Potomac
Trump's dream of redeveloping a municipal D.C. golf course into a championship-level venue is also temporarily on hold, despite his repeated social media pronouncements that the park would close and work would begin on Nov. 15.
Another D.C. district judge, Ana Reyes, intervened Saturday to order the administration to keep East Potomac Park open for two weeks, on the eve of its indefinite closure.
But the golf course itself is currently unstaffed, since its operator lease expired on Sunday. That hasn't stopped locals from showing up and teeing off, finding creative ways to mark the holes after the flagsticks were removed from the course.
Reyes has ordered both parties to weigh in on whether she has the authority to order the government to keep the golf course open.
On Wednesday, the Trump administration officially appealed Reyes' restraining order as it had promised. That order is currently set to expire on Nov. 28, the Saturday after Thanksgiving.
Noting that timing, the plaintiffs in the case — local golfers and historic preservationists — have asked Reyes to extend her order by another two weeks, until Dec. 12, while she considers the underlying legal issues and decides whether to issue a longer preliminary injunction.
The government, on the other hand, said "the court already has everything it needs to promptly consider a motion for preliminary injunction" and has proposed a schedule that would enable her to issue a final ruling by Nov. 28.

items.summary:
European leaders unite in Berlin to reaffirm support for Ukraine
German chancellor warns peace talks without Europe’s involvement are doomed to fail, urging unity with Ukraine.
European leaders of the so-called “Coalition of the Willing” gathered in the German capital for talks intended to signal a
items.text:
European leaders unite in Berlin to reaffirm support for Ukraine
German chancellor warns peace talks without Europe’s involvement are doomed to fail, urging unity with Ukraine.
European leaders of the so-called “Coalition of the Willing” gathered in the German capital for talks intended to signal a united front in support of Ukraine.
The Berlin meeting happened hours after an unprecedented three-way summit in Shenzhen, China, between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.
Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the Shenzhen meeting a “photo op”, warning that any deal made without Europe at the table would fail.
Merz said that “if it comes to peace negotiations, then we will be involved”, adding that such talks “can only be successful with Ukraine and Europe”.
Merz said he hoped to work as a “team with Kyiv and Washington” when they hold talks with Russia on ending the Ukraine war, although no announcement of when that would be has been made.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Europe is “ready to enter negotiations”, insisting that “a peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia must come first”.
“Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position,” Burnham added.
European countries have been angered after the European Union was largely sidelined in the United States’ stop-start negotiations with Russia and Ukraine.
However, Donald Trump’s son-in-law and peace envoy Jared Kushner said, “Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side.”
Kushner said, “We do believe that Russia having Europe at the table will be essential for ending the war.”
The British prime minister welcomed the US presence at talks in Berlin, saying it added momentum to end the war.
“This clearly has got to be a moment to move towards peace because of the US involvement that we’ve seen today and the progress clearly that is being made,” Burnham said.
Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron called on Ukraine’s allies to ramp up efforts to end the war.
“Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now,” he insisted, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.
“Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to NATO,” Macron said. NATO membership for Ukraine is among the issues holding back a peace deal for Ukraine.
In a post on X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, “We do not want Russia to drag all of this out into the winter. Pressure is needed. Europe is ready with new sanctions and new steps to support Ukraine and the Ukrainian people. It is important that the United States of America exert its influence on Russia.”

Issued on: Modified:
Gang of three or glorified photo op? Xi Jinping hosting Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Already, our Monday panel rejected attempts to paint the three-way meeting as a new Yalta, as in the 1945 sit-down on the Black Sea that defined the post-war security architecture of Europe.
We’ll ask if this was indeed little more than a PR exercise, what the leaders of China, Russia and the United States have in common. Could the trio even go full Yalta if they wanted to and carve up Ukraine? Kyiv sending quite the calling card to the parties in Shenzhen, knocking out Vladimir Putin’s jewel, the bridge that actually leads from the Russian mainland to Yalta in the Crimean peninsula.
And just to show Ukraine’s not alone, European backers staging what some have billed a counter summit in Berlin with that Franco-British led coalition that some have dubbed the coalition of the willing, others NATO without the Americans. A message of resolve for the Kremlin? A way of telling pro-Ukraine lawmakers in Washington that traditional allies are leaving the light on for them or to remind China - whose strength rests on its export-driven economy - that this old continent of ours buys a whole lot of the stuff that’s made in Shenzhen?
Produced by François Picard, Rebecca Gnignati, Juliette Laffont, Ilayda Habip, Léonore Jaury.

The United Nations’ top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, finding the military acted with “genocidal intent” and killed about 10,000 people during its 2017 operations in Rakhine state.
In a landmark judgement under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar in breach of its obligations — a decision Rohingya activists hope will finally bring accountability for years of mass killings, rapes and the burning of villages.
Nearly a million Rohingya fled those attacks, crossing into Bangladesh and building one of the world’s largest refugee settlements around Cox’s Bazar.
Today, many remain confined to overcrowded, fragile camps, stateless and with little prospect of safe return, even as the ICJ ruling sharpens pressure on Myanmar’s military and raises wider questions about justice for victims of mass atrocities.
This photo story returns to the early months of the crisis in 2017, documenting Rohingya families arriving exhausted and traumatised, queuing for food and trying to rebuild a semblance of community in the makeshift camps.
Through these images, all captured in September 2017, we see how the violence now recognised as genocide reshaped countless lives – and why, for Rohingya still living in limbo, the court’s judgement is only one step in a much longer struggle for safety, rights and a home.

items.text:
Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
November 19, 2026
Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.
"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods."
In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.
"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.
"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.
Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.
Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.
Ramping up electricity production
As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.
In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.
While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.
"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives."
Drilling for oil
At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.
Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.
The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.
Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.
"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way."
The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.
"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming."
Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.
Carbon trading 'breakthrough?'
Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough."
Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.
"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.
Carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.
"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.
"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed."
This interview also appeared as a video.

items.summary:
Blockbuster GTA VI release shows cultural, economic heft of video games
Runaway success of popular franchise comes as video game industry has struggled with mass layoffs in recent years.
Even before its release, Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) was a cultural phenomenon that cemented the status of video
items.text:
Blockbuster GTA VI release shows cultural, economic heft of video games
Runaway success of popular franchise comes as video game industry has struggled with mass layoffs in recent years.
Even before its release, Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) was a cultural phenomenon that cemented the status of video games as the undisputed champion of the vaunted United States entertainment sector.
The game racked up more than $1.5bn in pre-sales before Thursday’s launch and attracted nonstop buzz and anticipation on social media, where players have waited more than 13 years since the last edition of the popular franchise was released.
“The launch of GTA VI is a reminder that games aren’t just niche entertainment—they’re now at the centre of global culture,” Mark DeLoura, Vice President of Strategy for GDC Festival of Gaming, told Al Jazeera in an email.
In GTA VI, players follow the journey of two characters, Jason and Lucia, as they explore the underworld of Vice City, a fictionalised version of Miami, Florida.
Almost impossibly, the newest addition seems to have lived up to more than a decade of hype: critics are nearly unanimous in their praise, with the latest GTA becoming the best-reviewed video game of all time.
That success is partly explained by the nostalgia that the game evokes for those who grew up playing it with friends, along with meticulous worldbuilding and attention to detail, memorable soundtracks, and the transgressive thrill of running pedestrians over in a semi-truck.
GTA’s appeal was only heightened by the fact that, for an earlier generation of gamers, parents, media coverage, and politicians were united in stern disapproval.
While most critics of violent video games have long since abandoned the field or switched sides in a bid for relevance with young voters, a few holdouts remain.
“I really am going to say I’m not thinking this is a good thing for our culture and society,” a member of a recent Fox News programme said of the game.
“They’ll have a documentary on how best to steal a car at gunpoint or shoot a cop,” Republican Representative Tim Burchett told the outlet TMZ, arguing that GTA encourages violence and lawbreaking. “I mean, what in the world!”
But across US culture and politics, the taboo has largely faded away.
Once the subject of television segments asking if it would corrupt impressionable youths by exposing them to a seedy underworld of carjackings and police shootouts, everyone from the US military and the White House to the Weather Channel has tapped into the runaway popularity of the game’s sixth instalment.
The US military outlet Task and Purpose reported that 43 soldiers took advantage of a reenlistment incentive that gave them a four-day weekend to enjoy the game’s release.
Assessments of GTA’s cultural impact have also shifted, with critics lauding the franchise’s ability to capture the pulse of life in the US and its exploration of themes such as the hardships faced by immigrants and minorities.
“When a release like this becomes a major cultural event in the US and a shared global conversation, it says a lot about both the scale of the games industry and the place games now hold in people’s lives,” said DeLoura from GDC Festival of Gaming.
According to the Entertainment Software Association, an industry group, about two-thirds of people in the US play video games, and the sector generated more than $95bn in economic activity in 2025, with US consumers spending more than $60bn on games.
By comparison, the 2025 North American box office for movie ticket sales was just under $9bn.
Industry challenges
The runaway success of GTA VI comes, counterintuitively, at a time when the gaming industry is struggling to cope with a challenging financial environment and mass layoffs.
“The industry hired for a pandemic that ended. Demand stopped growing in 2022, costs didn’t, and the average blockbuster now costs $440m, up from $47m in 2000,” Joost van Dreunen, an adjunct assistant professor at NYU Stern and writer of the SuperJoost Playlist newsletter on Substack, said in an email.
“GTA VI proves that the model works for exactly one company,” he added, noting that the developer, Rockstar Games, spent a billion dollars and leaned on thousands of employees to create a level of attention to detail that few others can hope to match.
According to the tracker website Gaming Layoffs, 40 video game studios have shuttered in 2026 alone, with nearly 13,000 workers laid off. That figure represents a nearly 150 percent increase over the same time last year.
Life for some workers in the industry has also become more precarious.
A survey of industry workers by the GDC Festival of Gaming, compiled in a state-of-the-industry report in 2026, found that about 39 percent of US respondents had been laid off at least once in the last two years.
About 77 percent of US respondents also said they were “not hopeful” about the direction of the industry, and about 30 percent said they were considering leaving.
DeLoura from the GDC Festival of Gaming said the industry’s challenges have had “a real impact on a lot of very talented people”, but he remains optimistic the industry will weather the storm.
“The long arc of the game industry is one of strong growth,” he said.
“More people play games than ever, more people have access to them on the devices in their pockets, and more people can make and share games than at any point in history! To me, that’s the clearest way to understand this moment: not as a contradiction, but as a sign of how big, global, and varied games have become.”

items.title: NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from record one light-day away, 49 years after launch
items.summary:
NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from record one light-day away, 49 years after launch
The Voyager 1 probe launched by NASA nearly a half century ago has reached a distance from Earth of one light day (more than 26 billion kilometres), the farthest any human artifact has ever ventured from our planet. T
items.text:
NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from record one light-day away, 49 years after launch
The Voyager 1 probe launched by NASA nearly a half century ago has reached a distance from Earth of one light day (more than 26 billion kilometres), the farthest any human artifact has ever ventured from our planet. The space agency received a signal from the spacecraft Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent.
NASA’s Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away, humanity’s first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space.
Flight controllers received the spacecraft’s call Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent. That’s how long it took for the radio signal to traverse the more than 26 billion kilometres (16 billion miles) at the speed of light.
“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler,” NASA’s Joe Westlake, the heliophysics division director, said in a statement.
It marked another day in the history books for Voyager 1, which launched in 1977. It swept past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, snapped the most distant photo ever taken of our “Pale Blue Dot” in 1990, became the most distant human-made object in 1998, and crossed from the sun’s sphere of influence into the vast void between stars in 2012.
Read moreNASA's Voyager 1 leaves solar system
NASA could not confirm this newest distance record until the signal reached the control team at California's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. But that didn’t stop the space agency from wishing everyone a “Happy Voyager light-day … day!” via social media the day before.
“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” JPL director Dave Gallagher said in a statement.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, are NASA’s longest-operating space missions, still churning out data despite powering down most of their instruments to keep exploring.
Voyager 2 actually beat its twin into space by two weeks. But its route to Jupiter and Saturn plus Uranus and Neptune was slower and longer, and it did not reach interstellar space until 2018. It won’t reach the one-light-day mark until 2035.
Both spacecraft are doing well for their 49 years of age, plowing through space at 38,000mph (61,000kph) with plutonium for power. Picture-taking ended long ago, but they typically send back bits of precious data almost every day on their never-before-explored environment.
No science or engineering data have been received from Voyager 1 since Saturday, according to NASA. However, the carrier signal that normally conveys that data kept coming and, along with flight path calculations, allowed the team to confirm the light-day milestone. Controllers are trying to figure out why the flow of science and engineering data stopped.
Each carries a so-called Golden Record brimming with the sounds of Earth. The project was led by the late Cornell University astronomer Carl Sagan, who also coined the phrase “Pale Blue Dot” for Voyager 1’s farewell glimpse of Earth.
NASA expects the gold-plated phonographic records – time capsules for anyone or anything that might encounter them – to last more than 1 billion years.
For those tired of anxiety-inducing news, The Bright Side highlights initiatives, new discoveries and lighter perspectives to showcase progress and positivity in the world. Whether covering scientific innovations, inspiring profiles or striking images, our stories are always based on rigorously verified facts.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

items.summary:
Save the Children: Gaza’s children face ‘unmatched dangers’
Aid group says one third of violations against children worldwide were in occupied Palestinian territory.
Children in Gaza face dangers “unmatched” anywhere in the world after three years of war, with at least 20,000 killed, according to th
items.text:
Save the Children: Gaza’s children face ‘unmatched dangers’
Aid group says one third of violations against children worldwide were in occupied Palestinian territory.
Children in Gaza face dangers “unmatched” anywhere in the world after three years of war, with at least 20,000 killed, according to the aid group Save the Children.
The warning came in the group’s annual global report on Thursday – the same day Israel’s military told the AFP news agency it had finished a ground operation in central Gaza that began a day earlier, despite a “ceasefire” that took effect more than a year ago.
Save the Children said almost one third of the tens of thousands of attacks and violations against children recorded worldwide last year took place in the occupied Palestinian territory.
It counted nearly 12,500 cases – mostly attacks on hospitals and schools, and denial of aid.
“This report is showing very clearly that what happened and what continues to happen in Gaza are violations at a scale that we haven’t seen,” Regional Director Ahmad Alhendawi told the AP news agency.
He said conditions have shown little improvement this year, and that many surviving children are injured and have lost their parents.
The report found that denial of humanitarian aid is the fastest-growing violation against children worldwide. Verified incidents rose from 509 in 2015 to 8,322 in 2025 – almost one per hour on average – and more than 70 percent of them targeted Palestinian children.
Killings and maimings made up the largest share of violations since 2005, with 171,712 verified cases, and more than 70 percent were recorded in four countries, plus the occupied Palestinian territory.
Children waiting for treatment
Gaza’s Health Ministry said at least 300 children have died while waiting for Israeli permission to leave for life-saving treatment, including at least 90 with cancer. Another 5,400 are on medical travel lists awaiting approval. In February, it reported that 1,360 patients had died awaiting permits since the Rafah crossing between Gaza and Egypt closed in May 2024.
Displaced resident Riad Abou Shamel, 65, told AP that Gaza’s children “are deprived of the bare minimum in life”.
“They go to the market and can barely bring back half a cucumber or half an apple,” he said.
Israel ends incursion
Israel’s military told AFP that its first broad ground offensive since a “ceasefire” was signed more than a year ago “is complete”.
The new operation was launched in central Gaza on Wednesday, and went beyond the “Yellow Line” to dismantle a tunnel the Israelis claimed posed an “immediate and direct threat” to its troops.
The “Yellow Line” demarcates the Israeli-occupied area of Gaza, and was established under the truce agreed by Israel and Hamas in October 2025.
Hamas called the two-day operation a “blatant ceasefire violation”.
More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the “ceasefire” began, according to an AFP tally of Gaza Health Ministry data.
Israel did not immediately comment on Save the Children’s report, the AP said.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.
The landmark judgement in The Hague on Thursday is the first time a state has been held responsible for genocide at the ICJ.
The case filed by Gambia in 2019 has been closely watched by governments, lawyers, rights groups and Rohingya communities for its implications for how states are judged under the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The court said Myanmar has an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations it committed, with the terms to be determined at a later date.
Here’s how key parties and world leaders reacted to the landmark verdict:
Myanmar’s shadow National Unity Government
The National Unity Government, which includes remnants of former leader Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy party, said it respects the authority of the International Court of Justice and its judgement.
It pledged to consider the court’s findings and orders, reaffirming its commitment to accountability and preventing further atrocities.
The Gambia
The Gambia, which brought the case against Myanmar in November 2019 with the support of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, welcomed the ruling with “profound satisfaction”, calling it “a historic day for international justice”.
The government said the obligation to prevent and punish genocide is shared by all states party to the 1948 Genocide Convention and called on Myanmar to comply with the judgement “fully and without delay”.
Organisation of Islamic Cooperation
In a post shared on X, the OIC commended the ICJ’s judgement, saying it offered “redress for victims and [upholds] the principle of no impunity”.
United Nations Secretary-General
Antonio Guterres described the ruling as a “demonstration of international justice” and a reaffirmation that impunity for “such horrific acts must not stand”.
He noted that it marked the first time the court had found a state responsible for committing genocide and called on Myanmar to comply with its decision.
UN Human Rights Chief
Volker Turk said the judgement “clearly concludes” that Myanmar is responsible for “one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind.”
In a post shared on X, he added that the Rohingya people’s “suffering is a stain” on humanity.
UK Foreign Secretary
Ed Miliband said the United Kingdom ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defence attache and summoned the country’s charge d’affaires. He also called for an urgent UN Security Council session to discuss the ruling.
He said further measures would be announced in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held accountable.
UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar
Yanghee Lee called it a “deeply emotional day for all Rohingya people”, adding that “justice has been decided, but not yet delivered”.
Rohingya activist and co-chair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council
Activist Nay San Lwin said justice for the Rohingya means the restoration of their citizenship, recognition of their identity and their safe and dignified return home.
He added that their struggle would continue until those demands are met.
Rohingya activist and executive director of Women’s Peace Network
Activist Wai Wai Nu said the ruling had shattered the military’s decades-long efforts to erase Rohingya identity, deny their existence and dismiss their suffering.
“By finding that Myanmar committed genocide, ordering a guarantee of non-repetition, and ordering restitution and compensation, the world’s highest court has permanently shattered that state-sponsored lie,” she said.
Amnesty International
Human Rights Watch senior international justice counsel
Maria Elena Vignoli welcomed the court’s decision, calling it a “long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military”.
