items.title: World marathon champion Jepchirchir gets three-year doping ban
items.summary:
World marathon champion Jepchirchir gets three-year doping ban
- Published
Reigning world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been banned for three years for a doping violation.
The 33-year-old, who also won Olympic gold in 2021, was provisionally suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU)
items.text:
World marathon champion Jepchirchir gets three-year doping ban
- Published
Reigning world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been banned for three years for a doping violation.
The 33-year-old, who also won Olympic gold in 2021, was provisionally suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) in October after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for erythropoietin (EPO).
The sample was collected in Kenya prior to Jepchirchir winning the Sydney Marathon on 30 August 2026 and returned an adverse finding on 17 September.
She is one of three high-profile Kenyan athletes to have been sanctioned. Veronica Loleo has also been banned for three years after admitting using EPO, while Ronald Korir has received a six-year ban after failing to explain abnormalities found in his biological passport.
EPO is a natural substance produced within the kidneys that stimulates the creation of new red blood cells.
If injected, it increases the amount of red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles, in the blood stream but is only detectable in urine or blood for a short window of time.
Jepchirchir's other major wins came at the New York Marathon in 2021, the Boston Marathon in 2022 and the London Marathon in 2024.
While she denied using EPO, she signed an admission of violations form and accepted disqualification of all her competitive results since 17 July 2026.
"The Kenyan authorities have made a lot of progress in the fight against doping in the last five years, but these cases highlight that there is still a long way to go," said Brett Clothier, chief executive of the AIU.
"The Kenyan government is aware of the current situation and has committed to further strengthen the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya and take action to address the criminal networks that facilitate doping within the country.
"We will discuss the details behind these commitments with the Kenyan government in the coming months."
In September, Kenya was awarded the right to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships, with London and Rome missing out.
The decision increased scrutiny of the country's efforts to tackle a long-running doping problem, with more than 140 Kenyan athletes, predominantly distance runners, having been suspended by the AIU since 2017.
Last month Witold Banka, president of the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), told BBC Sport that Kenya must demonstrate it can be a "clean" home of athletics if it is to retain its credibility leading up to the 2029 event.
- Jepchirchir withdraws from London Marathon 
  - Published14 April
- Kenya must be 'clean' to be credible, says Wada chief 
  - Published7 October
'Reinforces concerns about integrity'
Jepchirchir's ban will deepen scepticism towards Kenyan athletes, including those competing cleanly, and further place the spotlight on athletics administrators and the government.
She is the second high-profile Kenyan athlete to be banned for doping in the past two years, following 2019 world champion Ruth Chepngetich, who was sanctioned last year.
The timing is particularly damaging. Jepchirchir's ban comes two months after Kenya won the bid to become the first African country to host the World Athletics Championships in 2029.
Kenya's bid was built on its rich history as an athletics powerhouse, producing numerous World and Olympic champions in middle and long-distance running but doping scandals threaten to overshadow that legacy.
The suspension of another high-profile athlete, who has won Olympic, World and major marathon titles, reinforces concerns about the integrity of Kenyan athletics.
The AIU has previously said the country's cases are isolated with no evidence of systemic violations. Local anti-doping officials say testing, investigations and sanctions have been strengthened in recent years.
However, recurring cases involving elite athletes raise questions about whether deterrence, education and efforts to prosecute those facilitating doping are keeping pace.
The growing number of positive tests could also reflect more effective testing and intelligence-led investigations, exposing violations that might previously have gone undetected. World Athletics president Sebastian Coe has previously acknowledged Kenya's progress, but says more work remains.
At the moment, Kenya has a proposed anti-doping bill before Parliament, whose passage and effective implementation could help reinforce its commitment to protecting the integrity of sport before 2029.
But legislation alone will not be enough. The ultimate test will be whether Kenya can effectively detect, sanction and prevent doping as it prepares to host the biggest athletics championships ever staged on African soil.

items.title: Race for the Fifa presidency: lineup revealed to challenge Gianni Infantino
items.summary:
Fifa has confirmed that Gianni Infantino will face challenges from Philippe Diallo of France and Japan’s Kozo Tashima in March’s presidential election.
The president of the French Football Federation and honorary president of the Japan Football Association submitted nomination letters with endorseme
items.text:
Fifa has confirmed that Gianni Infantino will face challenges from Philippe Diallo of France and Japan’s Kozo Tashima in March’s presidential election.
The president of the French Football Federation and honorary president of the Japan Football Association submitted nomination letters with endorsements from five member associations by Wednesday night’s midnight CET deadline. The former Switzerland and Tottenham defender Ramon Vega has not met that threshold, despite repeatedly saying he would stand.
“The candidatures have been forwarded to the electoral committee for examination and for passing a decision on the admission of the candidate,” Fifa said.
The election in Rabat on 18 March will be the first time Infantino has faced opposition since he was first elected in 2016, when he defeated the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88.
Infantino had been expected to be re-elected unopposed for a third time after declaring his candidacy in April and had received more than 200 letters of endorsement from national associations by the time of last summer’s World Cup, but the emergence of his Fifa Forward Enterprise plan has led to a haemorrhaging of support.
Uefa has led a campaign to unseat him since July with backing from Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, and initially the AFC, but with Infantino conducting a global tour to rally support from smaller nations they have struggled to put up an alternative candidate.
Tashima was the first to declare last month in defiance of the AFC, which after criticising the FFE proposal is backing Infantino, having come under pressure from the region’s two major financial powerhouses, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
As revealed by the Guardian on Monday, Diallo was belatedly chosen last weekend as the Uefa candidate after a complex selection process. The 63-year-old’s emergence was a surprise because Uefa had initially hoped to field a more high-profile candidate, such as Arsène Wenger. The Hungarian banker Sandor Csanyi, the president of his country’s FA, had strong backers owing to his close relationship with Uefa’s president, Aleksander Ceferin.
Diallo and Tashima may yet join forces in an attempt to defeat Infantino amid concerns of splitting those opposed to the president among the 211 Fifa members. Were that to occur it is expected Tashima would stand aside, a development that would be supported by Uefa.
All three candidates will be vetted by Fifa’s governance, audit and compliance committee, chaired by the Infantino ally Bruno Chiomento, before the nominations are confirmed on 18 February.

items.title: How 'sleeping giant' Everton are exceeding expectations
items.summary:
Everton: How Premier League's 'sleeping giant' are exceeding expectations ahead of Brentford test
After a difficult summer, Everton are proving greater than the sum of their parts with another European push and some battling performances; watch Brentford vs Everton live on Sky Sports Premier League
items.text:
Everton: How Premier League's 'sleeping giant' are exceeding expectations ahead of Brentford test
After a difficult summer, Everton are proving greater than the sum of their parts with another European push and some battling performances; watch Brentford vs Everton live on Sky Sports Premier League and Main Event from 6.30pm on Monday Night Football; kick-off 8pm
Thursday 19 November 2026 11:14, UK
Everything felt a bit gloomy at Everton after the closure of the summer transfer window. 'Disappointment' was the buzzword used by David Moyes - especially after a Deadline Day move for Folarin Balogun fell through.
Moyes has said for some time that the Toffees need more bodies, but for all of his public declarations, Everton have been left with just 18 senior players and one recognised striker until January.
Coming so soon after a late-season collapse saw them miss out on European football, it is understandable why Moyes was left frustrated and some tipped them for relegation form.

- Everton fixtures & scores | FREE Everton highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
"My expectations changed during the window," the Scotsman said recently. "I don't think Everton are ever going to spend hundreds and hundreds of millions to improve so all I can do is take a small progression, get a bit better every year and that felt it was going to be much harder, but the players are doing a brilliant job with their league position."
Any expectations have been exceeded. Everton are mounting another European push, currently sixth in the Premier League - just two points from the top four. They are also into quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup, facing Fleetwood in the final eight next month.
"It's a massive club, a sleeping giant of the English game," Everton midfielder Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall told Sky Sports. "I really want to do something with this club or win some silverware and give the fans something to scream about."
While it remains early in the season, the belief and confidence is clear. The Toffees are proving greater than the sum of their parts as their upward trajectory under Moyes continues.
Everton don't know when they are beaten
It hasn't all been easy points for Everton - they have had to work hard for them. In two draws against Bournemouth and Manchester United, they did not score before the 83rd minute. They needed an 80th minute goal from Charly Alcaraz to beat Wolves in the third round of the Carabao Cup.
The Toffees also went behind to Coventry in their last Premier League match before the international break, going on to win 3-1. Admittedly, that game came with its own dose of luck for Everton, but fans might argue that it is about time they were on the right end of things.
After that game on Friday Night Football, Dewsbury-Hall said: "Our mentality this year has gone from strength to strength... we just never know when we're out of the game. Every time we have gone behind this season, we've reacted in a positive manner."
And just as importantly, they have seen out games when needed. There have been wins and clean sheets against Crystal Palace, Ipswich and Newcastle. They also swept the Magpies aside in the Carabao Cup fourth round with a convincing 3-1 win.
They have only lost twice - at home to Chelsea and away to Premier League champions, Arsenal. Neither result was disastrous.
In-form players boosting attacking output
After beating Newcastle in the Premier League, Moyes said: "We're creating chances. That's the big thing for me. We want to be a side that creates more chances. If we could be more offensive, that's the way I'd like it to be."
And Moyes is getting his wish. Everton are largely matching or exceeding their numbers from last season. While the number of goals scored per games is roughly the same, they are registering more shots and have a higher xG.
A big part of that is down to the form of their only recognised striker Thierno Barry. "He's come back off the summer like a different player," team-mate Dewsbury-Hall said.
He is playing far more centrally than last year - where he spent more time on the right wing - and is close to surpassing most of his attacking numbers from the entirety of last season with only ten games played. He has also scored in three successive games for Everton for the first time. Suddenly, the Frenchman is discovering a taste for goals that even the most optimistic Evertonian would have struggled to predict.
However, he has missed more big chances than any other Premier League player this season (16) - twice as many as the player in second, Bournemouth's Rayan (8). It suggests he has actually been anything but clinical, and if he had a better finishing touch, he could be an early frontrunner for the Golden Boot. His continued improvement in that part of his game is going to be vital for Everton.
Another in-form playing having a huge influence is Dewsbury-Hall himself.
Sky Sports pundit Jamie Redknapp was full of praise for the midfielder after his display against Coventry, especially in the No 10 role, running forward with and without the ball to push Everton up the pitch.
"I'm really enjoying it," the former Chelsea and Leicester man said of his role in that game. "I've got a really good hybrid role in this team where the gaffer has given me license to pop up all over the pitch.
"I feel like I'm getting a good relationship with Thierno now and I'm buzzing he keeps getting the goals because he deserves it so much... as long as he keeps performing, I'll keep trying to help him as much as I can."
The Moyes factor
Moyes is the Premier League's most experienced manager. Monday's game at Brentford will see him overtake Harry Catterick's record of the most Everton games managed, moving on to 493.

The 40-year-old former Manchester City captain was taken
items.text:
'I'm very healthy' - Kompany to return to dugout after health scare
- Published
Bayern Munich boss Vincent Kompany says he is "very healthy" and grateful for all of the support he has received as he prepares to return to the dugout on Friday.
The 40-year-old former Manchester City captain was taken to hospital after falling ill while watching the club's second team train last month.
Kompany was diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
Speaking at a news conference on Thursday he thanked the club, medical staff, players, coaches and fans for their support.
"It was very intense," he said.
"At the time, it was a new experience. Looking back, everything went perfectly. I received support right away, from the club and the doctors. I'm very grateful.
"You try to stay calm and wait until you have the results. It was a positive process, all the tests were positive.
"I have to say, I'm very healthy. We did a lot of tests, and they all came back fine. In those quiet moments, you also try to learn.
"Now I feel very good again and I'm happy to be back with the team."
While he has been recovering Kompany's assistant Aaron Danks has led the side to four wins and a draw.
Bayern, for whom England captain Harry Kane has been in fine form, are top of the Bundesliga, level on points with Borussia Dortmund.
Defending champions Bayern face Cologne on Friday after the end of the two-week international break.

South African DJ Lag says it is a "dream come true" to have his music featured on Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), the hugely popular video game released on Thursday.
DJ lag, one of South Africa's best-known electronic
items.text:
'It's a dream come true' – South African DJ celebrates featuring in GTA 6
- Published
South African DJ Lag says it is a "dream come true" to have his music featured on Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), the hugely popular video game released on Thursday.
DJ lag, one of South Africa's best-known electronic music producers, is among several African stars to feature, alongside Nigerian singers Burna Boy and Asake.
"I can't explain the feeling. I started playing the game last night and it's amazing," DJ Lag told the BBC's Newsday programme, adding that he had been playing GTA since he was about 10 years old and could hardly believe he was now part of the latest edition.
Many players have already had a chance to play the game following its worldwide launch.
The game, which lets players explore a fictional American city, features a dedicated African music radio station playing Afrobeats, amapiano and other sounds from across the continent.
The release of GTA 6 ends a 13-year wait for a new edition of the game.
Rockstar Games, the developer behind the franchise, has revealed details of the game's soundtrack and some in-game radio stations, but has yet to release a complete list of songs featured in the game.
Rockstar says AfroBank FM features everything from 20th Century African classics to contemporary amapiano and 3-step, giving the continent's music a prominent place in the latest edition.
Burna Boy co-hosts the station alongside British DJ and producer Palms Trax, while Asake's hit song Joha is among the tracks players can listen to as they drive around the game's virtual world.
DJ Lag, whose real name is Lwazi Asanda Gwala, is regarded as one of the pioneers of gqom, a genre of electronic dance music that emerged in the port city of Durban in the early 2010s.
He posted on Instagram: "God did."
Ghanaian highlife legends Pat Thomas and Ebo Taylor also feature, alongside South African artists Robot Boii and Kamo Mphela, bringing a mix of classic and contemporary African music to one of gaming's biggest franchises.
Rockstar has also announced a 34-track official soundtrack album, released in partnership with Atlantic Records, featuring an original Burna Boy song titled Bigger.
For African fans, the inclusion of familiar music adds another dimension to the experience, allowing players to hear some of the continent's biggest sounds while exploring the American setting.
The series allows players to roam through sprawling fictional cities, drive vehicles and complete missions involving crime, police pursuits and other adventures.
The latest instalment takes players to Vice City, a fictional version of Miami, and the surrounding US state of Leonida, inspired by Florida.
Its story follows two criminals, Jason and Lucia, who become caught up in a wider conspiracy after a robbery goes wrong.
The launch has generated enormous excitement among gamers around the world.
Some fans downloaded it in advance so they could begin playing as soon as it became available, while others have booked leave from work.
The previous edition, GTA 5, was one of the best-selling video games of all time, selling more than 200 million copies worldwide.
The new release is expected to be another major commercial success, although it remains to be seen whether it will match its predecessor's extraordinary sales.

Will Infantino feel he's already won as Fifa challengers confirmed?

Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will take on incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.
World football's governing body has confirmed the three candidates for the election, which will take place at the Fifa Congress in Morocco on 18 March.
European football's governing body Uefa only identified its candidate Diallo fewer than 48 hours before Wednesday's deadline.
French Football Federation (FFF) president Diallo, 63, received the unanimous support of Uefa's executive committee.
Japan Football Association honorary president Tashima, 68, announced his intention to stand against Infantino, 56, earlier this month.
Tashima is a member of the Fifa Council and a former international footballer and coach.
Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega had also said he intended to stand but was not named as a candidate by Fifa on Thursday.
A late and surprise choice, Diallo said: "I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative...I'm entering this campaign not just to provide a different voice, but to win."
But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.
Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he possessed the credibility to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.
But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.
So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?
- FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on 
  - Published14 hours ago
- Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino 
  - Published3 days ago
- Japan's Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency 
  - Published5 November
'A fantastic advocate for change'
An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.
In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.
According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.
"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.
"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."
Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).
However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.
Has Uefa lost momentum?
While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer," he admitted.
Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.
Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."
They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.
Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."
McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said.
"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."
Infantino win inevitable?
Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.
As recently as August it all seemed very different. Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour strongly criticised Infantino for the FFE scheme, while a senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned. The heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - then signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".
Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered a series of setbacks.

Eight-year ban for player who threw rock that hit assistant referee
- Published
An Ecuadorian footballer has been banned for eight years for throwing a rock at an assistant referee, leaving him requiring surgery to his face.
Jhon Perlaza was playing for Club Ciudad de Yantzaza against Club Rio Aguar
items.text:
Eight-year ban for player who threw rock that hit assistant referee
- Published
An Ecuadorian footballer has been banned for eight years for throwing a rock at an assistant referee, leaving him requiring surgery to his face.
Jhon Perlaza was playing for Club Ciudad de Yantzaza against Club Rio Aguarico FC in a third-tier match in October when the incident took place.
The stone struck assistant referee Lenin Giovanni Ojeda Nunez in the face in the 96th minute of the game, which was subsequently abandoned.
A video on social media shows Perlaza standing up in the team's dugout to throw the stone, with Nunez instantly falling to the floor and holding his face after the object hits him. He then receives medical attention.
"The assistant referee suffered serious injuries that required surgery and a 60-day recovery period," the Ecuadorian Football Federation (FEF) said.
"The disciplinary committee found the player responsible for physical aggression against a match official and suspended him for eight years from all football-related activity, until 19 October, 2034.
"In addition, the FEF will ask Fifa to extend this sanction worldwide."
The FEF also fined his club Yantzaza $2,000 (£1,521) and ordered them to pay Nunez's medical fees of $4,369 (£3,323).
In a statement released on 20 October, three days after the match, Yantzaza apologised to the refereeing team and the fans, and confirmed Perlaza had been sacked as a result of the incident.
"As an institution, we categorically reject all acts of aggression, whether verbal or physical, both inside and outside sporting venues. We firmly believe that football should be a space of respect, coexistence, and fair play," they said.
"Once the person responsible for this regrettable incident was identified, the institution made the decision to remove him immediately, and he is therefore no longer part of our club."

items.title: Five return for Wales' World Cup play-off final
items.summary:
Five return for Wales' World Cup play-off final
- Published
Ceri Holland has been named in the Wales squad for next month's Women's World Cup play-off final against Norway despite being out since September through injury.
Olivia Clark, Hayley Ladd, Rhiannon Roberts and Ella Powell are also included
items.text:
Five return for Wales' World Cup play-off final
- Published
Ceri Holland has been named in the Wales squad for next month's Women's World Cup play-off final against Norway despite being out since September through injury.
Olivia Clark, Hayley Ladd, Rhiannon Roberts and Ella Powell are also included after fitness issues, but Ffion Morgan, Laura Hughes and Scarlett Hill are among those who miss out with injuries.
The versatile Holland, arguably Wales' most influential player, has been out with a muscle problem, though she is thought to be close to returning to action for club side Liverpool.
Her involvement is a major boost for Wales as they attempt to reach the Women's World Cup for the first time.
Rhian Wilkinson's side face Norway at the Cardiff City Stadium on Tuesday, 1 December, before the return leg in Oslo four days later.
Wales v Norway
Women's World Cup qualifying play-off final first leg
Tuesday, 1 December at 19:15 GMT
Cardiff City Stadium
Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.
Leicester goalkeeper Clark and Sunderland defender Roberts are also included even though they have not played since September, but the loss of promising Manchester United defender Hill is a blow given her impressive displays against Albania.
Crystal Palace's Ladd and Powell, of Bristol City, have played for their clubs since missing Wales' World Cup play-off semi-final games against the Albanians last month.
Winger Morgan had returned to action for West Ham after not being involved against Albania, but she is back on the sidelines after suffering a knee injury while playing for the Hammers last weekend.
Like Southampton midfielder Hughes, Mia Ross – who is without a club after leaving Charlton in September - is missing again, while Fulham full-back Charlie Estcourt is another absentee.
There is also no place for Sunderland defender Tara Bourne, who has switched allegiance from England to Wales but is injured.
There is a recall for once-capped teenager Gwen Zimmerman, who plays for American side Northwestern NCAA, while Newcastle youngster Casi Gregson is included again after winning her first cap against Albania.
- Wales start Nations League with home double-header 
  - Published5 days ago
- Wales in fight to retain rising female stars 
  - Published1 November
Wolves midfielder Chloe Williams keeps her place having been a late call-up for the semi-final, while the only uncapped player in the squad is third-choice goalkeeper Soffia Kelly.
Wales are hoping to cause an upset as they bid to reach the Women's World Cup for the first time, though beating former champions Norway may not be enough to guarantee a place in Brazil next summer.
The complex nature of the qualification process means that Wales may have to negotiate inter-confederation play-offs next February to secure a World Cup place, even if they triumph over Norway.

items.title: FIFA confirms Infantino rivals for 2027 presidential election
items.summary:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino is officially facing two election opponents trying to end his 11 years in office.
Philippe Diallo of France and Kohzo Tashima of Japan met the midnight deadline in Zurich to file entry papers with nomination letters from five member federations, FIFA confirmed on Thur
items.text:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino is officially facing two election opponents trying to end his 11 years in office.
Philippe Diallo of France and Kohzo Tashima of Japan met the midnight deadline in Zurich to file entry papers with nomination letters from five member federations, FIFA confirmed on Thursday.
The vote by FIFA's 211 member federations will be held on March 18 in Rabat, Morocco.
Infantino's critics, led by UEFA, have been trying to replace him since his secretive plan to sell stakes in World Cup profits to private investors was revealed in July. He dropped the project amid a fierce backlash.
"(T)he candidatures have been forwarded to the electoral committee for examination and for passing a decision on the admission of the candidate," FIFA said in a statement.
FIFA has set a Feb. 18 deadline for its three-member election panel to tell the 211 members which candidates are approved to go on the ballot paper.
Candidates must pass an eligibility and integrity check by the panel, whose rulings can later be challenged at the Court of Arbitration for Sport in Lausanne, Switzerland.
Infantino also received heavy critism for FIFA's handling of the red card shown to United States striker Folarin Balogun during last summer's World Cup which resulted in his ban being overturned after an intervention by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Former Liverpool manager Jürgen Klopp has said he thinks Infantino should be replaced as FIFA president.
"There is now a unanimous consensus that a change would make sense," Klopp, now the Germany head coach, said this week.
"I thought that, after Sepp Blatter, the situation couldn't get any worse -- but here we are."
Who is Philippe Diallo?
The French Football Federation president, who played in Nantes' academy, has worked in football since 1992 and was a judge in FIFA's dispute resolution chamber for more than 20 years.
He said he has received "strong signs of support from other continents" when launching his bid for the FIFA presidency in Paris on Tuesday.
Diallo said the first figure from UEFA to push him to mount a challenge to Infantino was English FA chair Debbie Hewitt.
The 63-year-old has said he will try to convince his presidency rival Tashima to "join forces," but did not detail exactly what that might mean for their respective candidacies as they try to oust Infantino.
Who is Kohzo Tashima?
Tashima, 68, is the first person from Japan to run for FIFA presidency.
"It's not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built," he was quoted as saying by Reuters as he announced his intention to run for FIFA president.
"What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world."
He has been on FIFA's ruling committee since 2015 when Sepp Blatter was president.
Previously, Tashima was a footballer for Japan and head of his nation's federation. As a player, he earned seven Japans caps in 1979-80.
Associated Press contributed to this story.

WASHINGTON -- North Carolina Courage forward Ashley Sanchez was named the 2026 NWSL Most Valuable Player on Wednesday after scoring a record-tying 20 goals this season.
"Coming back from some tough years, to have something like this, it's just incredible," Sanchez told reporters outside the at Lisne
items.text:
WASHINGTON -- North Carolina Courage forward Ashley Sanchez was named the 2026 NWSL Most Valuable Player on Wednesday after scoring a record-tying 20 goals this season.
"Coming back from some tough years, to have something like this, it's just incredible," Sanchez told reporters outside the at Lisner Auditorium on the campus of George Washington University, where the NWSL Awards Show was held. "And I think, for me, this year I've just proved to myself what I'm capable of. I think I was just really consistent, and that's something that I've always wanted out of my play, and I accomplished that."
Sanchez's 20 goals tied the NWSL record set in 2024 by Kansas City Current forward Temwa Chawinga, who also won the MVP and Golden Boot award that year. Sanchez also had five assists and led the NWSL with 25 goal contributions. Her 20 goals this season were more than her first five NWSL seasons combined.
She was traded to the North Carolina Courage from the Washington Spirit in January 2024 in a trade that she said at the time took her by surprise.
Sanchez also had a difficult 2023 World Cup, when she made the United States' roster and appeared to be in line for a prominent role, but did not play a single minute. She held back tears as she discussed her journey on Wednesday.
"I always felt confident in what I could do, but I knew that I had some things to work through to get here," Sanchez said. "And it was just all part of the journey, and I knew that was what was going to happen. It was kind of on me to figure out how to navigate myself out of that."
Sanchez has been a phenom since her early teenage years. In 2016, she became the first American player to compete at a U17 World Cup and a U20 World Cup in the same year. She is only the second player in the NWSL's 13-season history to win MVP on a team that failed to make the playoffs.
Chawinga, Washington Spirit forward Trinity Rodman, Denver Summit defender Janine Sonis and Portland Thorns FC forward Sophia Wilson were also finalists for the MVP award. Rodman and Chawinga will face off in Saturday's NWSL Championship across the city at Audi Field.
The Kansas City Current's Croix Bethune won the Midfielder of the Year award for the second time in three years. Her 11 assists set a new single-season NWSL record. Sonis was named the Defender of the Year after scoring 12 goals and adding eight assists from the fullback position for Denver Summit FC.
Gotham FC's Ann-Katrin Berger won the Goalkeeper of the Year award after recording 11 shutouts, second most in the league.
Jimmy Coenraets was named the NWSL Coach of the Year after leading the Utah Royals to their first playoff appearance. The Royals defeated the San Diego Wave FC in their first franchise playoff game to advance to the semifinals, where they lost to the Washington Spirit.
Gotham FC forward Jordynn Dudley was named the Rookie of the Year, marking the third time in four years that a Gotham player has won the honor.
Angel City FC defender Savy King won the Lauren Holiday Impact award for establishing Savy King of Hearts, a nonprofit focused on CPR awareness, preventive screenings, and heart health advocacy. King started the foundation after her own on-field cardiac emergency during a match in 2025, when she received life-saving intervention from medical staff and athletic trainers. Doctors discovered a heart abnormality after she was brought to the hospital.

items.title: Uganda deadly landslide survivors seek justice at the UN
items.summary:
Uganda deadly landslide survivors seek justice at the UN
- Published
Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.
The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitut
items.text:
Uganda deadly landslide survivors seek justice at the UN
- Published
Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.
The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.
Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.
The landslide struck Bududa in 2019, killing more than 53 people, including 33 children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.
William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family members.
"My quest should be a lesson," he said.
"Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens."
The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods.
"I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.
The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.
They are seeking compensation for lost family members and livelihoods, as well as emergency measures, including accessible early-warning systems in high-risk areas.
Greenwatch Executive Director Samantha Atukunda Kakuru Mwesigwa said the case is about changing how governments prepare and respond to climate-related disasters.
"Justice for claimants is not just about winning in court. It is about forcing government policy to keep pace with a changing climate, and ensuring loss and damage is no longer an afterthought in disaster management," she said.
The threat of climate-related disasters extends across East Africa.
In Kenya, floods and landslides killed at least 181 people between March and May 2024, according to the Kenya Red Cross. In Rwanda, floods and landslides killed 135 people in May 2023.
The dangers are also being felt further afield. In October 2026, a flash flood swept through Nepal's Gorkha district after a landslide blocked a river, washing away homes and infrastructure, and killing over 1,500 people.
"Disasters like the one in Bududa are only getting worse because of climate change – and they are happening all around the world, as we've seen recently and tragically in Nepal," ClientEarth lawyer Vesselina Newman said.
She said poorer countries, which have contributed relatively little to global emissions, are bearing some of the heaviest consequences of climate change and need greater financial support.
"High income countries must provide financial assistance and ensure that sufficient money goes directly to countries like Uganda, so they can roll out life-saving adaptation measures," she said.
Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.
The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.
But the complainants say relocation must involve more than move people out of danger.
They want the government to protect their livelihoods, respect their land rights, and take account of individual needs.
The case is now before the United Nations Human Rights Committee, which will ask the Ugandan government to respond within six months.

items.title: Dozens missing after boat carrying 100 migrants sinks off Senegal's coast
items.summary:
Dozens missing after boat carrying 100 migrants sinks off Senegal's coast
- Published
Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the coast.
Initial reports said that one person had died, but some local media have reported
items.text:
Dozens missing after boat carrying 100 migrants sinks off Senegal's coast
- Published
Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the coast.
Initial reports said that one person had died, but some local media have reported that at least four bodies have been recovered. Dozens of people are still missing.
Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.
This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.
Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).
"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.
A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, the AFP reported.
Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.
At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.
He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.
Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.
Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.
The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.
It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.
As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.
They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.
Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.
They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.
On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.
It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

There is no one-size fits all when it comes to determining great strikers, but they do all share a common trait - a ruthlessness in front o
items.text:
The best European strikers this century - ranked by you
- Published
Classic number nines, penalty-box poachers, troublesome targetmen and tireless all-rounders.
There is no one-size fits all when it comes to determining great strikers, but they do all share a common trait - a ruthlessness in front of goal.
This week, however, we put the power in your hands to decide the best European frontmen of the 21st century.
Tens of thousands of you voted on the 20-man shortlist drawn up by our panel.
We then asked European football experts Guillem Balague, Julien Laurens and Raphael Honigstein to discuss your choices on the Euro Leagues podcast.
So from 10-1, here are the best European strikers this century - as voted for by you.
10. Karim Benzema
Karim Benzema comes in at number 10, the former Lyon and Real Madrid frontman's closest challengers coming from across the continent in the shape of Raul, Robin van Persie, Michael Owen and Miroslav Klose.
Laurens: "From a young age you could see he was something special. I know it was difficult at the beginning at Real Madrid, but in the post-Cristiano era he carried that team, wore the armband and won big titles and trophies by being decisive in big moments. Like I used to say 'Karim the dream'."
Honigstein: "The selflessness, the ability to work for the team. A sense of elegance and humility on the pitch, which is unusual in a goalscorer. I think he is unusual in that list. I think not many will define themselves through their teamwork and assists as much as their goals, but he was that player."
9. Ruud van Nistelrooy
Ruud van Nistelrooy edges Benzema, with whom he briefly overlapped at Real Madrid - the Dutchman teed up the Frenchman and scored himself in their only La Liga appearance together, before he left for Hamburg in January 2010 following injury problems.
The former PSV striker's most consistent spell, of course, came at Manchester United, where he scored 150 goals.
Honigstein: "He is the nicest guy but he never came across that way on the pitch. Typical trait of a striker, he would kill to score the goal. I think anyone who has grown up with him scoring goals, for United especially, must have a soft spot for him because he was a phenomenal poacher."
Laurens: "He was a strong player physically, and despite the lack of pace the awareness in the box was just very special even with all the injuries."
8. Zlatan Ibrahimovic
Zlatan Ibrahimovic slots in at eight, comfortably clear of Van Nistelrooy and Benzema. The Swede netted more than 500 times in a career that spanned Malmo, Ajax, Juventus, both Milans, Barcelona, Paris St-Germain, Manchester United and LA Galaxy.
Balague: "He was a big-game player and that explains the league titles with PSG. Scoring four goals against England, the overhead kick. The personality thing has put him one or two places in this list, saying 'I am great, I am the best'. If you keep saying you're great it makes people stop and think."
Laurens: "The mentality of really believing he was the best and nobody was better than him, apart from maybe Brazilian Ronaldo, who was his idol growing up, and he would watch videos of him and try to replicate in his council estate. If you watch a highlight reel of his best goals he was incredible."
Honigstein: "What makes him unique among the strikers is his technique, You could see elements of martial arts in his goals. No-one scores goals like that."
7. Wayne Rooney
The first Englishman on the list, although the third to have represented Manchester United - it's the Old Trafford outfit's record goalscorer, Wayne Rooney.
Honigstein: "I don't think there is anyone who would've watched English football at that time [early in his career] and not been enthralled by his game. The only downside is the combination of injuries and not the most professional lifestyle meant he did not fulfil his potential. He could've been Messi."
Balague: "What could have been, yes. He was the national team's record scorer too before Harry Kane took it. I find him to deserve this place as he had to adapt to a lot of strikers and he did it well. He had the ability to link up and score. He was very intelligent."
Laurens: "He is the most street footballer England has ever seen. There's no rules, that kind of anger you saw on the pitch. I don't think people in England realise how good he was."
6. Kylian Mbappe
What does becoming the all-time World Cup top goalscorer get you? Sixth place on the best European strikers this century list. The Real Madrid forward, 27, just misses out on the top five.
Laurens: "Maybe if we do this ranking again in a few years he will be higher. I would have had him top five, for sure. He has scored more than 400 goals. I don't think Messi and Ronaldo had scored that many at that age, so he's ahead. I don't know if he will play for as long as them but he hasn't done much wrong in his career."
Balague: "This list has to do what you feel about the player, not science - 22 goals in 22 appearances in World Cups and [Euro] Championships. He should be at least top three because of that. Great stats, but we're not in love with him."
Honigstein: "I don't think there is a forward that is as good as footballer as him in 2026. On that basis alone he should be higher, but people when they vote have other things in their head. The only way to win everyone over is to score more goals and win more World Cups for France, which I think is possible."
5. Erling Haaland
There was little between Mbappe and Erling Haaland, but it is Manchester City's prolific Norwegian who slips in at fifth. The 26-year-old has already scored more than 300 club goals and has a staggering 68 in 61 games for his country.
Balague: "Mbappe should be higher than him. Haaland scored 52 goals in 53 games [in 2022-23], that is astonishing, but he's gone 11 finals without scoring. We're talking about the best. We're talking about what we see at the moment and what we see is someone who is calculated but in a more charming way. An abilit

items.title: Joshua unable to see new baby daughter until after Fury fight
items.summary:
Anthony Joshua: British heavyweight boxer becomes dad for second time but unable to see daughter until after Tyson Fury fight
Anthony Joshua says ongoing training camp for his fight against Tyson Fury on December 11 means he will not see his new-born daughter until the days after the fight; "It's no
items.text:
Anthony Joshua: British heavyweight boxer becomes dad for second time but unable to see daughter until after Tyson Fury fight
Anthony Joshua says ongoing training camp for his fight against Tyson Fury on December 11 means he will not see his new-born daughter until the days after the fight; "It's not ideal but she is in good hands", says Joshua, who describes daughter's arrival as a "big blessing"
Thursday 19 November 2026 11:17, UK
Anthony Joshua became a father for the second time after the birth of a daughter last weekend, although ongoing training for his fight against Tyson Fury means he is not able to see her until mid-December.
Joshua, whose son JJ was born in 2015, is currently in training camp in Marbella in preparation for his blockbuster all-British fight against Fury on December 11 at Cardiff's Principality Stadium, and was unable to be at the birth.
Joshua says the arrival of his daughter, who has not yet been named, is "amazing" and "a big blessing" as the 37-year-old paid tribute to Nicole, the mother of both children.
- Opetaia withdraws from Wilder bout on Fury-AJ undercard
- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW📺
- Listen to the Toe2Toe podcast every week
While he has been able to have "many" FaceTime calls with mother and daughter in recent days, Joshua says he wished he would have been able to be there but preparations for the Fury fight mean mean he is currently "on a mission".
"It's not ideal but she is in good hands," Joshua said in an interview with The Sun.
"She's got an amazing mother, she's got amazing family round her and the people at the hospital, I heard they were amazing. I spoke to them and said thank you, so I'm pretty content at the minute that she's in good hands. But, for me, it would have been much better if I was able to be there.
"But I'm on duty at the minute and we're on a mission. I knew about this nine months ago so I made this commitment that I can't change, unfortunately, but there will be many more birthdays I'll be at, for sure."
Asked when he would likely meet her in person for the first time, Joshua said: "Probably December 12, December 13.
"I'll go and check in and rock her to sleep, let her hear my voice and let her feel my heartbeat, really. The basic stuff."
He said he would be a fully hands-on father.
"I'm going to do it all. I'm going to definitely do it all," he added.
"You might see me with some eye shadow on, some nail polish on, drinking some tea in a doll's playhouse just trying to do the right thing by her."
Joshua said he had wanted to become a father for a second time to "do something positive" after the "painful and traumatic" experience of last December's car crash in Nigeria that killed two members of his team, personal trainer Latif Ayodele, and strength and conditioning coach Sina Ghami.
"After the year that I'm coming off I wanted to do something positive," said Joshua, who was injured in the crash.
"I wanted to give JJ the opportunity to be an older brother. One day I won't be here and he'll have a sibling that he can turn to, be with and plan their future together. It's nice to have a sibling that they can lean on each other when needed, when me and his mum aren't here one day in the future."
The British boxer added: "Nicole is doing good. She is healthy. She said it was an amazing experience. She said it was easier than JJ and she's much prettier than JJ, so she's happy! She's already deeply in love with her."

items.title: Maine Road offer non-league haven to fans of scandal-hit Manchester City
items.summary:
It began with a timely message on social media. “We’ve seen the posts. We’ve read the comments. If all the recent conversation has made you curious about the other team in Manchester playing in sky blue, come and see us.”
It was a direct response to the news of a guilty verdict in the Premier League
items.text:
It began with a timely message on social media. “We’ve seen the posts. We’ve read the comments. If all the recent conversation has made you curious about the other team in Manchester playing in sky blue, come and see us.”
It was a direct response to the news of a guilty verdict in the Premier League’s financial fair play case against Manchester City and it came from the 10th-tier (step six) club Maine Road, who carry City’s colours and a near-identical badge, as well as the name of City’s previous home.
Maine Road stadium was demolished in 2003-04 and replaced by houses but two miles away, in a corner of Chorlton-cum-Hardy, Maine Road FC are playing in front of about 100 people on a cool November Saturday. The high-stakes surroundings of the Premier League seem a fair distance away, but Maine Road – founded in 1955 in Rusholme as a Manchester City supporters’ club team – have never professed to be City.
“There is FC United and Manchester United, who are intrinsically linked in terms of why that club exists,” says Rob McKay, Maine Road women’s head coach, watching as a fan as the men’s side draw 0-0 with Halewood Apollo in the North West Counties League First Division North. “This is not a protest club. The links with City have ebbed and flowed over the years. It’s just that they were playing out of the Maine Road social club when it formed.”
The chair and director Alex Simmonds, who arrived in the summer, has big ambitions for Maine Road. He believes the fallout from City’s legal battle with the Premier League could help attract a new audience.
“It was a bit of a statement,” Simmonds says of that social media post. “We came across a lot of comments when the news came out and a lot were saying: ‘Well, we’ll stop watching City if they get relegated or if anything happens, and we’ll just go to Maine Road.’ That came up in quite a few conversations online.”
Simmonds admits there has not yet been a huge rise in crowd numbers, with City fans, perhaps understandably, staying defiantly loyal to their club, who have appealed against the independent commission’s verdict. His priority is to regenerate Maine Road. “For me coming into the club, it was about trying to get people to see that we are here,” he says. “To get in touch with the community and to get fans down here, so no matter who you support in the Premier League or Championship or whatever, we are here.”
Maine Road offer free entry to anyone with a season ticket for a Premier League or EFL club, hoping to boost numbers during international breaks or when other Greater Manchester teams play away. Simmonds is helping to fund a multimillion-pound renovation of St Margaret’s Community Centre, which serves as Maine Road’s clubhouse. The club are also launching a new website and a scheme to hand out thousands of free tickets to local primary schools.
Will that, combined with potential disillusionment after any City punishment, bring fans flocking to Maine Road? “I think it will,” Simmonds says, “but only if people know that there’s a difference between a Premier League Man City and a Maine Road at step six. If they come with ideas that we are going to be a City or even one of the bigger semi-pro teams … we’re not quite there yet. But their support would help.”
Non-league football in Greater Manchester has enjoyed a significant surge in popularity since Covid, so Maine Road find themselves in a crowded marketplace. McKay says: “West Didsbury and Chorlton are down the road and they get 1,000. Droylsden get huge crowds, Ashton United get huge crowds, Curzon Ashton are getting reasonable crowds. There’s so much football.”
Simmonds believes the connection with City, however loose, should help Maine Road gradually gain a foothold. City’s former training ground at Platt Lane is a stone’s throw from Brantingham Road, where Maine Road play. City’s academy teams have played at Maine Road’s ground, as well as at nearby St Bede’s College.
Another connection is the fact Maine Road are managed by a former City player in Leon Mike, who made his only City start at the old Maine Road in 2001 under Kevin Keegan.
“People make jokes about the Etihad not being full, but genuinely, a lot of times you speak to City fans, they’ll say it’s too expensive,” says Mike. “Premier League, FA Cup, League Cup, Champions League, that’s a lot of games to go to. Whereas on a Saturday here it will cost you £6 to attend and you can have a pint and some food.”
There is optimism among those most closely connected with Maine Road that the club will soon experience growth. “We gained 9,000 followers across the platforms just on the back of that one social media post,” Simmonds says. “It was surprising – I didn’t think it would do that – but social media is really powerful. We’re definitely going to try and stay in that conversation and get people coming through.”

Man City vs Fulham: Cottagers ideal opponents to get City back to winning ways
Are Man City in crisis heading into Saturday lunchtime's clash against Fulham, with Enzo Maresca's side having lost their previous three Premier League contests to lose top spot to Arsenal?
Those trio of reverses against Aston Villa, Brighton and, just prior to the international break, Nottingham Forest, mean City have now lost as many times as in their previous 36 league outings.
Since the start of 2007-08, though, City have only been beaten in four successive top-flight games on two occasions, in August 2008 and December 2024, and it would take a massive leap of faith to suggest Fulham are the team to inflict such ignominy on them this weekend.
In fact, if Maresca could pick one side to face to get back to winning ways, it would be Fulham, who City have got the better of in each of their last 17 Premier League encounters, scoring at least twice each time.

Aston Villa vs Sunderland: Can Villa recover after sour note or will Black Cats begin to build?
Aston Villa left for the international break on a sour note after squandering a two-goal lead on two occasions at Old Trafford for their dramatic 4-4 draw against Manchester United.
Sunderland, meanwhile, secured a much-needed 1-0 win against Chelsea to relieve the pressure on Regis Le Bris.
His side remain in the bottom three because of their poor start to the season and a win at Villa Park is a big ask, especially given injuries to Granit Xhaka and Brian Brobbey, but it will be needed if talks of his departure are going to fizzle out.
The Black Cats have not travelled well this term with just one win on the road, which came in their narrow escape at Portuguese second-tier side Torreense, but Villa Park's crackling atmosphere has been dampened by the closure of the North Stand this season.
Injuries, storylines and ramifications. Plus, if it is anything like their last meeting at Villa Park, a dramatic 4-3 win for Villa courtesy of Tammy Abraham's injury-time winner, then this is one you will be wanting to follow along in the Sky Sports live blog.
Pat Rowe
Coventry vs Palace: Manager bounce or manager bump? Eagles might be in for a nasty surprise
The managerial merry-go-round is spinning again. Crystal Palace have jumped aboard, handing Thomas Frank the keys to Selhurst Park. New hope. But a new manager doesn't necessarily mean new results.
In fact, recent evidence suggests quite the opposite for teams in trouble.
The famous 'new manager bounce' is one of football's most romanticised theories. A fresh face walks through the door, standards supposedly rise overnight and points start rolling in.
Shame the numbers don't back it up.
Of the last six Premier League teams sitting in the bottom eight to change manager between November and March, five actually saw their points-per-game average drop across the following five matches.
Vitor Pereira at Nottingham Forest. Igor Tudor at Tottenham. Rob Edwards at Wolves. Graham Potter at West Ham. Ivan Juric at Southampton.
It's a fascinating trend that should serve as a warning to Palace supporters expecting Frank to arrive waving a magic wand.
The reality is that struggling teams usually have deep-rooted problems that can't be solved by a few tactical tweaks and an inspirational team talk. Confidence, structure and, ultimately, quality of players tend to outweigh a difference voice in the dugout.
Coventry are next up for Palace and Frank will be desperate to buck the trend.
But history suggests the bounce might be more of a bump.
Lewis Jones
Bournemouth vs Forest: Can Cherries pick up one more win to make club history?
Bournemouth couldn't buy a Premier League victory in the opening six weeks or so of the season, but over the last month they have looked like an unstoppable force. Now they can't stop winning.
Since a 3-0 win over Sturm Graz in the Europa League on October 15, the Cherries have won four in a row in the Premier League, three in a row in Europe and once in the Carabao Cup, booking a spot in the quarter-finals.
Eight wins in succession in all competitions; a club record equalled.
It's made even more astonishing when you realise Marco Rose has only been in charge for 16 games. And that it's the club's first ever season in Europe. And that those eight wins came within a period of just 25 days.
With the schedule that lies ahead, the run will naturally come under threat sooner rather than later, but where's the harm in trying to squeeze out one more win to make history?
Dan Long
Tottenham vs Ipswich: Stop Enciso, stop Tractor Boys?
Ipswich have a Julio Enciso problem. Not because the Paraguayan isn't delivering the goods. Quite the opposite. He's become so influential to their attacking output that stopping him is the key to stopping Ipswich.
Bournemouth certainly cracked it before the international break.
Their 2-1 victory over Ipswich was a tactical lesson in how to suffocate a team reliant on one creative spark. Cut off the supply lines into Enciso, deny him the space to weave his magic and ask the rest of the Ipswich attack to come up with the answers.

items.text:
Max Verstappen says he trusts F1 bosses over plans to proceed with season-ending races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi amid conflict in Middle East
Max Verstappen has backed F1's plans to proceed with the final two races of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi; the Red Bull driver had previously expressed doubts; watch the Las Vegas GP on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday and the race at 4am on Sunday
Thursday 19 November 2026 08:21, UK
Max Verstappen says he trusts Formula 1 to "make the right call" as the sport pushes on with plans to hold the final two races of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi despite continued conflict in the Middle East.
F1 had to cancel races scheduled in April in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, but the Qatar Grand Prix from November 27-29 and Abu Dhabi Grand Prix from December 4-6 are currently set to go ahead.
While F1 bosses had maintained throughout the year that their intention was to proceed with the events as planned, it was only after the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on November 8 that a contingency plan to hold a season-ending race in Italy was aborted.

Therefore, Wednesday evening's media sessions ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, which forms a season-ending triple header with the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, was the first opportunity for the drivers to publicly react to the latest developments.
Red Bull's Verstappen, who had in September voiced his opposition to ending the season in the Middle East, appears to have changed his position.
The four-time world champion said on Wednesday: "I trust F1 and FIA to make the right call on that, right?
"I don't have all the intel. I'm not an officer. I just hope that they make the right call on that. And that's all that you can rely on, really.
"They also send over their findings and understanding. So I trust them."
While there haven't been notable recent incidents in Qatar or Abu Dhabi, a US military base in Bahrain was targeted over the weekend, and Houthi rebels in Yemen are advancing in their war against the country's Saudi Arabian backed government.
Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc acknowledged that the situation remains "tricky" but also expressed faith that F1 and the sport's governing body, the FIA, will act responsibly.
"It's a situation that is kind of tricky," Leclerc said. "At the same, I feel like we are up to date with whatever is organised, and I guess that on our side we have to trust the process, and that's what I'll do.
"I'm sure the FIA is taking everything seriously to make sure that everybody is safe. It's in the best interest of absolutely everyone.
"So, yeah, me as a driver, I'll just trust that process, and be in Qatar if it's safe to be there."
Norris, Russell reassured by friends in region
British drivers Lando Norris and George Russell both said they have been reassured by friends of theirs who live in the Middle East.
Russell often represents his rivals in his role as a director of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association (GPDA), but he explained that the seriousness of the situation has resulted in that organisation having little involvement.
"We're [the GPDA] not involved because it's way above our heads, and the truth is, we will be going if nothing is escalated," the Mercedes driver said.
"F1 is not making those decisions, it's the people in the high powers of politics.
"I trust in Formula 1. I'm not concerned. I know a lot of people who live in the region, and they say pretty bluntly, 'we're living there with our families, and if we didn't feel safe, we wouldn't be.'
"They feel safe as it is, and I'm sure and I hope everything will be ok."
Norris revealed that he will be attending a friend's wedding in Bahrain ahead of the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, but said he was more concerned for members of his McLaren team than himself.
"I have my friend's wedding in Bahrain next week, so I was planning on going there and then going on to Qatar and then Abu Dhabi," the 2025 world champion said.
"But it's not about me. It's a lot more people. It's the fans, it's the team personnel, so the question is for them, more than I would say it is for myself."

items.title: How Premier League's big six keep getting richer
items.summary:
How Premier League's big six keep getting richer
- Published
Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top six spots are occupied by 'big six' clubs.
Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton,
items.text:
How Premier League's big six keep getting richer
- Published
Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top six spots are occupied by 'big six' clubs.
Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.
In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.
The six biggest clubs - Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.
And the gap is growing. Every season.
BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.
Big six get richer and the gap grows
Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.
In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.
Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.
This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.
Let's look at how the gap has grown.
We will use Everton, the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.
This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.
In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was £120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to £442m.
So what has driven this huge escalation?
In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.
Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.
"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.
"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."
Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.
It means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.
For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.
But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.
Champions League widens the gulf
It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.
This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.
But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.
When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.
This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or £713m, for the historically most successful clubs.
At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned £37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool £35.5m and Chelsea £33.3m. Newcastle received only £13.6m.
The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.
Their value pillar is projected to be worth £25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.
The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.
Stamford Bridge - Chelsea's big problem
Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.
In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.
Not just by a small amount. They were £74m behind Tottenham, and £200m below Liverpool and City.
Chelsea's problem is simple - seats.
Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the big six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.
Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of £80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.
Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.
"Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.
"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast."
Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only £16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by £69m and Spurs, thanks to their new ground, by £85m.
"Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.
"Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial."
Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.
But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.
How new rules allow big six to spend even more
You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).
PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.
